summary: Updates the handling of DirectoryString in the Internet X.509 certificate and CRL profile from RFC 3280. UTF8String and PrintableString are preferred, and a requirement for exclusive use of UTF8String after a date is changed. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 5280.

eli5.summary: Certificates have to write names as text. This changes which text formats are required so everything keeps working.

subtitle: Fixing how text is encoded in digital certificates and revocation lists

tldr.problem: RFC 3280 required all certificates issued after 2003 to use UTF8String encoding for names, but this deadline had already passed and created problems for interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: This update removes that deadline and allows CAs to use either PrintableString (for ASCII-range characters) or UTF8String (for international characters), with backward compatibility for older encoding methods.
tldr.outcome: The change simplifies certificate creation and improves compatibility with existing deployed certificates, though it was later superseded by RFC 5280.

today: RFC 4630 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 5280, which consolidated and updated the X.509 certificate profile specification.

sections.title: The Problem with RFC 3280
sections.content:
RFC 3280 defined the rules for digital certificates (the documents that prove you are who you say you are on the internet). One of those rules was how to encode the names inside certificates: names like "Example Company" or "John Smith." At the time RFC 3280 was published, internationalization (supporting languages other than English) was poorly understood, so the specification required that all certificates issued after December 31, 2003 MUST encode names using UTF8String, which supports any language.

However, by 2006, that deadline had already passed, and the requirement was causing problems. Many older certificates still used other encoding methods like PrintableString or BMPString. The absolute requirement for UTF8String was breaking interoperability with existing systems, and many certificate authorities could not comply.

This RFC updates RFC 3280 by removing the UTF8String-only requirement and aligning the specification with what was actually working in practice.
sections.eli5: An old rule said all certificates made after a certain date had to use one specific text format. But that date already passed and it was causing problems, so this changes the rule to be more flexible.

sections.title: How Names Should Be Encoded
sections.content:
The RFC specifies three types of fields that contain names: the Issuer field (who created the certificate), the Subject field (who the certificate is for), and the Subject Alternative Name extension (an additional way to name the certificate's subject).

For all three, the new rule is the same: certificate authorities MUST use either PrintableString or UTF8String when creating new certificates. PrintableString covers basic ASCII characters (letters, numbers, spaces, and some punctuation), while UTF8String covers any Unicode character and thus supports all world languages.

The one exception is backward compatibility: if a CA has previously issued certificates with old encodings like TeletexString or BMPString for a particular subject or issuer, the CA MAY continue using those old encodings for that same subject or issuer in new certificates, to avoid breaking name comparisons in certification paths.

The RFC also notes that legacy systems sometimes incorrectly use TeletexString to encode ISO 8859-1 (Latin1) characters, and implementations should be prepared to handle both correct and incorrect interpretations.
sections.eli5: Use modern text formats (PrintableString for simple names, UTF8String for any language). If you have old certificates with different formats, you can keep using those formats for the same person, but do not start using them for new people.

sections.title: Security and Name Matching
sections.content:
Using consistent encoding for name components is important for security. Certificate systems rely on name constraints and name matching to work correctly. If the same name is sometimes encoded as PrintableString and sometimes as UTF8String, the system might treat them as different names, breaking the security properties of certification paths.

The RFC advises that any name components appearing in both the Subject field and the Issuer field SHOULD use the same encoding throughout the certification path to avoid confusion.

A subtle security issue arises from the fact that different text encodings can produce visually identical characters. For example, the character é can be written as a single precomposed character or as e plus an accent mark. Two different names might look identical to a human but be encoded differently in the certificate. Certificate issuers and relying parties both need to be aware of this possibility and use care when comparing names visually.
sections.eli5: Use the same text format for the same person throughout a chain of certificates, so the system recognizes them correctly. Also, be careful because some names can look identical but actually be different.

sections.title: Migration Strategy
sections.content:
RFC 3280 included an exception for name rollover certificates, which allow an orderly migration from old to new encoding. A CA can issue a certificate where the issuer field uses the new UTF8String encoding but the subject field uses the old encoding (or vice versa). This lets existing systems gradually migrate to the new preferred encodings without abrupt breaks.

The specification also notes that when creating a distinguished name, the CA MUST ensure the subject field (the recipient of the certificate) contains a non-empty name that matches the issuer field of subsequent certificates issued by that subject. This maintains the consistency of the certification path.
sections.eli5: Old and new text formats can be mixed in special migration certificates to help systems transition smoothly. Names must match up properly across the chain of certificates.
